summary: Pre-mortem (AI estimate): on today's path Caplet most likely misses the Top 50 not because of its strategy but on the criteria only students can earn. The bar is about 2% (49 of 2,339 reports last season; main-page counter re-verified 16 Oct) and Wharton wants teams that score 'exceptionally well on all five components', so the weakest criterion decides; Caplet has ~700k words of AI research on its strongest criteria and a 421-word journal that stops 7 Oct. Ranked failure stories: (1) Final Report written in the last days, thin Articulation and projections (~25%; last year 30 of 63 dated comments came in the final two days); (2) voice reads as AI (~20%; V5 is 'AI generated' by the team's note and the 16 Oct [AI] rule invites more, while the IPS bans citations); (3) competent but not memorable (~15%); (4) the IPS locks rules that protect the range (99.4%) better than the payments (6.3% of paths short after 2033), with 'cannot miss' and no certainty definition (~15%); (5) numbers and claims disagree across the three documents (~8%); plus noise, gate failures and integrity flags. New: the number sheet's open 'pick one' protection choice changes what the IBTM and VT reflections can say, so it must be decided by Tue 20 Oct, not 6 Nov; and none of the 15 Oct brief's repo-visible actions was done in the 16 Oct commit, which reversed its first item. Ladder conflict re-run: $294,461 (room $5,539) prices an ideal ladder to 1 Jan payment dates on a forward basis; $298,628 (room $1,372, 4.7bp) prices Caplet's actual maturities with yields unchanged; use the holdings basis for every Caplet claim, and since one day (14-15 Oct) moved the cost $2,635, state the top-up rule rather than a forecast. Reverse pre-mortem: a winner would have one student-written rulebook repeated identically in all three documents, the most honest co-sponsor uncertainty message in the field, and six students who can each defend a number live with a true story of change. Stop: new AI research waves, WInS value tracking, activity trading, AI mock-judge scores, humanising AI drafts or detector tests, extra Monte Carlo precision, more PDFs, name debates, last year's four-category rubric, and over-polishing the TNA.
